'''Walter Rudin''' (May 2, 1921 – May 20, 2010<ref name="MadisonWSJ">{{cite news|url=http://host.madison.com/wsj/news/local/education/university/article_b6fa8098-6512-11df-9cbf-001cc4c002e0.html|title=Noted UW-Madison mathematician Rudin dies at 89|newspaper=Wisconsin State Journal|date=May 21, 2010|last=Ziff|first=Deborah|access-date=May 21, 2010}}</ref>) was an [[Austria|Austrian-]][[United States|American]] [[mathematician]] and professor of mathematics at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Remembering Walter Rudin (1921–2010)|journal=Notices of the AMS|year=2013|volume=60|issue=3|pages=295–301|url=http://www.ams.org/notices/201303/rnoti-p295.pdf|doi=10.1090/noti955|last1=Nagel|first1=Alexander|last2=Stout|first2=Edgar Lee|last3=Kahane|first3=Jean-Pierre|last4=Rosay|first4=Jean-Pierre|last5=Wermer|first5=John|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In addition to his contributions to [[complex analysis|complex]] and [[harmonic analysis]], Rudin was known for his [[mathematical analysis]] textbooks: ''[[Principles of Mathematical Analysis]]'',<ref>{{Cite book|title=Principles of Mathematical Analysis|last=Rudin|first=Walter|publisher=McGraw-Hill|year=1976|isbn=007054235X|edition=3rd|location=New York|orig-year=1953}}</ref> ''Real and Complex Analysis'',<ref>{{Cite book|title=Real and Complex Analysis|last=Rudin|first=Walter|publisher=McGraw-Hill|year=1987|isbn=0070542341|edition=3rd|location=New York|orig-year=1966}}</ref> and ''Functional Analysis.''<ref>{{Cite book|title=Functional Analysis|last=Rudin|first=Walter|publisher=McGraw-Hill|year=1991|isbn=0-07-100944-2|edition=2nd|location=New York|orig-year=1973}}</ref> Rudin wrote ''Principles of Mathematical Analysis'' only two years after obtaining his Ph.D. from Duke University, while he was a [[C. L. E. Moore instructor|C. L. E. Moore Instructor]] at MIT.  ''Principles'', acclaimed for its elegance and clarity,<ref name=":1" /> has since become a standard textbook for introductory real analysis courses in the United States.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Locascio |first=Andrew |date=13 August 2007 |title=Book Review: Principles of Mathematical Analysis |url=http://www.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/principles-of-mathematical-analysis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150825054136/http://www.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/principles-of-mathematical-analysis |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 25, 2015 |access-date=12 October 2016 |publisher=Mathematical Association of America}}</ref>

Rudin's analysis textbooks have also been influential in mathematical education worldwide, having been translated into 13 languages, including Russian,<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/344.34419762320|title=Principles of Mathematical Analysis|last1=Rudin|first1=Walter|translator-last1=Havin|translator-first1=V. P. |publisher=Mir Publishers|year=1976|location=Moscow|edition=Russian translation of 2nd}}</ref> Chinese,<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/RudinW.1979_201704|title=Principles of Mathematical Analysis (simplified Chinese translation)|last1=Rudin|first1=Walter|translator-last1=Zhao|translator-first=Cigeng |translator-last2=Jiang|translator-first2=Duo  |publisher=People's Education Press, China Machine Press (reprint, 2004)|year=1979|isbn=7-111-13417-6|location=Beijing}}</ref> and Spanish.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Principles of Mathematical Analysis (Spanish translation)|last1=Rudin|first1=Walter|translator-last1=Irán Alcerreca Sanchez|translator-first1=Miguel |publisher=Libros McGraw-Hill|year=1980|isbn=968-6046-82-8|location=México}}</ref>

==Biography==

Rudin was born into a [[Ashkenazi Jews|Jewish]] family in [[Republic of Austria (1919–1934)|Austria]] in 1921. He was enrolled for a period of time at a Swiss boarding school, the [[Institut auf dem Rosenberg]], where he was part of a small program that prepared its students for entry to British universities.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rudin |first1=Walter |title=The Way I Remember it |date=1992 |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |isbn=9780821872550 |page=39}}</ref> His family fled to [[French Third Republic|France]] after the [[Anschluss]] in 1938. 

When France [[Armistice of 22 June 1940|surrendered to Germany]] in 1940, Rudin fled to England and served in the [[Royal Navy]] for the rest of [[World War II]], after which he left for the United States. He obtained both his B.A. in 1947 and Ph.D. in 1949 from [[Duke University]]. After his Ph.D., he was a [[C. L. E. Moore instructor]] at [[MIT]]. He briefly taught at the [[University of Rochester]] before becoming a professor at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] where he remained for 32 years.<ref name="MadisonWSJ" /> His research interests ranged from [[harmonic analysis]] to [[complex analysis]].

In 1970 Rudin was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Nice.<ref>Rudin, Walter. [http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1970.2/Main/icm1970.2.0489.0494.ocr.pdf "Harmonic analysis in polydiscs."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160924204424/http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1970.2/Main/icm1970.2.0489.0494.ocr.pdf |date=2016-09-24 }} Actes Congr. Int. Math., Nice 2 (1970): 489–493.</ref> He was awarded the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]] for Mathematical Exposition in 1993 for authorship of the now classic analysis texts, ''Principles of Mathematical Analysis'' and ''Real and Complex Analysis.''  He received an honorary degree from the [[University of Vienna]] in 2006.

In 1953, he married fellow mathematician [[Mary Ellen Rudin|Mary Ellen Estill]], known for her work in [[set-theoretic topology]]. The two resided in [[Madison, Wisconsin]], in the eponymous [[Walter Rudin House]], a home designed by architect [[Frank Lloyd Wright]]. They had four children.<ref name="Wisc obit" />

Rudin died on May 20, 2010, after suffering from [[Parkinson's disease]].<ref name="MadisonWSJ" />
